source.title: A Tale of Two Circuits: Grokking as Competition of Sparse and Dense Subnetworks
source.authors: William Merrill; Nikolaos Tsilivis; Aman Shukla

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks and analyzes its internal structure, using sparse parity and subnetwork measurements rather than the original modular-arithmetic setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from its own sparse-parity and binary-operator experiments. Claims about natural tasks, language models, or other work cited in the introduction and conclusion are not results of this study and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own networks and reports delayed generalization on sparse parity, and on Power et al.'s addition and division tasks. It also tracks internal measures (effective sparsity, subnetwork norm, faithfulness) across the transition. The task, model and measures differ from the originals' modular-arithmetic Fourier analysis, except for the division replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, at least in their sparse-parity setting, grokking arises from competition between a dense subnetwork dominating memorization and a sparse one that takes over. This is driven by selective norm growth of the sparse neurons and decay of the others. They speculate the sparse net implements a DNF-like parity construction. They argue the dense phase is not strict memorization, since addition generalizes via commutativity before grokking.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse parity with a 1-layer ReLU network and a pruning-based active-subnetwork analysis; it also includes binary addition and division experiments. It does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports a smaller weight-decay setting (λ = 0.001) and a larger parity size (k = 4) as additional configurations. Addition and division differ in pre-grokking test generalization.
record.peer_reviewed: Published at the Workshop on Understanding Foundation Models at ICLR 2023
record.problems: The main sparse-parity results use 5 random seeds and a fixed test set of 100 points. Many plotted outcomes are qualitative rather than reported as exact numbers. Training-set size is not varied, and the study does not establish the exact algorithm represented in each sparse subnetwork.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. The cited findings from other papers are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: The dependence of the delay on training-set size: N is fixed at 1000 for parity and 9400 for the operators.
Fourier-algorithm formation and continuous Fourier progress measures.
Weight decay is never removed or compared as a cause. No critical dataset size, no ungrokking, no efficiency comparison of circuits.
The exact algorithm in each run is not identified, and architecture and hyperparameters are not varied systematically.

missing.what: Larger parity size (40,4) configuration: accuracy, loss, sparsity, subnetwork norm and faithfulness, reported as consistent with the main findings.
Sparsity transition is computable from training data alone yet correlates with the test-accuracy transition.

record.verdict_notes: This is a workshop paper. Most evidence is qualitative and read from figures, with 5 seeds and a 100-point test set. The V5 attributions to weight decay are interpretive, with no no-weight-decay control, so no V5 verdict is given. The division experiment is close to the original Power et al. setup and provides a T1-like replication of V1.

versions.untested_parts: It does not vary training-set size to test whether smaller sets require more optimization.
It does not test the Fourier algorithm or continuous Fourier progress measures. It studies neuron norms, pruning-defined subnetworks, and prediction agreement instead.
No non-algorithmic task or initialization-scale/lazy-to-rich intervention is tested.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning experiment is conducted.
The study does not test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below it, and does not directly compare the efficiency of sparse and memorizing solutions across dataset sizes.

The study considers sparse-subnetwork sizes and possible parity constructions, but does not identify the exact algorithm implemented in each run or vary architecture and hyperparameters systematically.
No optimizer-instability or floating-point/softmax artifact control is tested.

rows.subject: 1-layer ReLU net
rows.operation_detail: Measure effective sparsity as the number of neurons in the active subnetwork.
rows.value: The network becomes orders of magnitude sparser as it starts generalizing; the sparsity transition coincides with the loss transition.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 2 shaded areas show randomness over training-set sampling, model initialization, and SGD stochasticity (5 random seeds).
rows.note: The authors attribute the sparsification to norm regularization after the data-fidelity loss is almost zero.
rows.check: The sparsity transition coincides with the loss transition rather than building gradually ahead of it, so it does not anticipate the jump as V2 says. The V5 link is only the authors' attribution to weight decay; no weight-decay control is run. Drop V5.

rows.subject: 1-layer ReLU net
rows.operation_detail: Track average neuron norm for the neurons in the final sparse, generalizing subnetwork.
rows.baseline: Similar average norm to the other neuron groups up to slightly before the grokking transition
rows.value: The generalizing subnetwork's norm begins to grow rapidly slightly before the grokking transition.
rows.note: The paper describes this as selective norm growth associated with emergence of the sparse subnetwork.
rows.check: Subnetwork norms are similar until slightly before the transition, then grow rapidly. That is a short lead, not gradual formation. The V5 link is interpretive with no manipulation; drop V5.

rows.subject: decoder only transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on the binary addition operator task and measure test accuracy.
rows.value: Above chance before grokking; the paper says it matches the level obtainable by using commutativity and looking up memorized training points.
rows.note: The authors attribute pre-grokking generalization to addition's commutative property.
rows.check: Above-chance pre-grokking accuracy (explained by commutativity) is not the opposite of grokking; a later jump to full generalization still occurs. Reversed is wrong; partial fits. Note that 9400 sample points is nearly all 97²=9409 pairs, which is unusual and may be a stated value worth checking.

statements.correction: Generalizing-neuron norm rises rapidly slightly before grokking; effective sparsity and faithfulness change around grokking. Verdict for this study: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The sparse-parity description is accurate, but challenges overstates this study's evidence: neuron norm does provide a short lead, and these measurements do not directly establish absence of gradual algorithm formation.
